problem: Existing VLN requires verbose step-by-step instructions and ignores global spatial priors like floor plans, which are ubiquitous in real buildings; agents cannot read or use them, and no dataset pairs floor plans with concise instructions.
motivation: Humans use floor plans to plan routes and only need to specify start region, goal region and stop condition. Offloading spatial complexity from language to a lightweight floor plan prior enables more natural human-robot interaction and avoids costly scan-and-reconstruct mapping. The challenge is aligning abstract floor plans, egocentric views and concise instructions.
key_idea: Rasterize semantic floor plans with visual prompts, render the agent's pose/trajectory on them, concatenate side-by-side with the egocentric frame per timestep, and finetune an MLLM (Qwen2.5-VL) with auxiliary region/trajectory/summary tasks to navigate from concise region-level instructions.
insight: How floor plan and observation are fused matters greatly: the aligned dual-view early fusion gets 20.9 SR versus 2.5-4.2 for static, dual-stream or interleaved inputs. Masking the floor plan (SR 20.9 to 12.3) or giving a random one (9.1) shows the model actually uses the plan. Auxiliary tasks add about 3 SR (17.8 to 20.9), and unfreezing the vision encoder gives a large gain (SR 20.9 to 25.9) because the ViT must adapt to symbol-dense floor plans.
method: Floor plan rasterization: vectorized region polygons (type, id) are rendered as images with type-coded colors and numeric id labels (visual prompting), since point encoders were hard to align with MLLM space.

Spatio-temporally aligned dual-view: each frame M_t = [O_t || G_t], where G_t is the floor plan with historical trajectory and current pose (oracle pose in sim, LiDAR odometry in real) rendered; uses a video of h=6 frames.

Auxiliary tasks: region localization (caption + region type via polygon query), trajectory reasoning (visited region history, current region, next region/stop condition), instruction summarization (reconstruct the concise instruction from the video).

Unified NTP training: navigation and auxiliary QA are trained jointly with cross-entropy and task-balanced sampling; actions are merged (consecutive forward/turn) and stop is upsampled; ~350K action QA + 174K region/trajectory QA + 9K summarization QA.
Noise modeling: actuation noise (move, rotation, drift), floor plan global scale noise and vertex jitter are simulated to test robustness.

FloorPlan-VLN dataset: floor plans from Matterport3D, trajectories from R2R-CE/RxR-CE filtered to single-floor, waypoints labeled with region ids/types, concise instructions generated by Qwen2.5-VL with 10 templates.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-7B (fine-tuned; FP-Nav frozen ViT, FP-Nav-v unfrozen ViT)
setting.training_data: FloorPlan-R2R (~9k episodes, ~350K action QA + ~174K aux QA + 9K summarization QA); FP-Nav-v-rxr adds ~1.7k long FloorPlan-RxR episodes (>10 m)
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB at 1 fps, concatenated with rendered floor plan image with agent pose/trajectory
setting.action_space: low-level MoveForward 25 cm / Turn 15° / Stop (merged actions at training, decomposed at inference)
setting.privileged: oracle agent pose from simulator to render on floor plan; GT vectorized floor plans with region types/ids; instruction gives start/goal regions

numbers_note: FloorPlan-VLN is a new benchmark not in the canonical list, so entries use other: names. Only main FP-Nav variants listed; noise and ablation tables are omitted.
results: On the new FloorPlan-VLN benchmark, FP-Nav beats the finetuned Navid-ft baseline (Val-Unseen R2R SR 20.9 vs 17.0), and FP-Nav-v-rxr reaches SR 28.8 / SPL 24.0 on R2R val-unseen and 25.2 on RxR val-unseen, well above zero-shot StreamVLN (14.6 SR). It is robust to moderate actuation and floor plan noise and reaches 24.0% SR in real-world deployment vs 8.0% for Navid-ft.
limitations: Relies on oracle pose (sim) or LiDAR odometry to render the agent on the floor plan; no self-localization from the plan itself.
Single-floor navigation only; absolute success rates remain low (about 25-29% SR unseen), and the real-world test is small (25 episodes, one building).
Floor plans are derived from Matterport3D annotations, and concise instructions come from templates, so the domain gap to real architectural drawings is only partly tested.
